transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-12-15
Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~42m
Location: Zoom — ClearPort POC weekly sync
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (SE), Diego (SRE), Nina (PM), Owen (ML Eng), Lena (Infra), Rajiv (CTO)

Summary (auto): short recap — plateau observed in throughput at 1.2k rps of small-token requests, intermittent latency spikes under mixed loads; plan: tune continuous batching + adjust max_inflight/queue_depth and run a controlled stress test.
Topics: continuous batching behavior, concurrency ceilings, queue/backpressure smoothing, burst fallback (dedicated -> hosted fallback), telemetry to collect.

Transcript:
[00:00:04] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll try to keep this tight, we have the results from last week's tuning and a couple of config suggestions from Jordan.
[00:00:12] Nina: great, thanks. short agenda? we mostly want to understand why we're seeing the plateau at ~1.2k rps for our small payloads and the occasional 5xx when long requests arrive.
[00:00:25] Jordan: yep, good framing. quick note, there's some OCR/auto-transcript stuff so names might get mangled. i pulled the pilot telemetry into a joint sheet and highlighted the tail latencies.
[00:00:38] Owen: ok, on our end we saw a steady CPU/gpu utilization around 72-80% on the dedicated nodes, but the request queue length hit spikes and then we got backpressure and timeouts.
[00:00:50] Diego: i think you're hitting a mix of two things: continuous_batching aggressive windowing + a conservative max_inflight. when a few long prompts enter, the batching tries to fill larger batches and that pushes shorter requests into queue. queue_depth and backpressure settings then drop some inflight requests.
[00:01:08] Rajiv: can you clarify continuous_batching windowing — is it time-based or size-based in Redwood's runtime? we've seen different behaviors across other vendors.
[00:01:20] Jordan: it's hybrid — time-first, with an adaptive size limit based on recent token length distribution. so if you suddenly send several 1.5k token requests, the runtime biases toward filling those batches which increases batch latency for small requests. that's when queue lengths rise.
[00:01:40] Nina: right, that's what we think we saw. small quick requests for search recs spiked, then a 2–3 long-generation jobs started and things slowed.
[00:01:49] Maya: key knob to look at: reduce batch max_wait_ms for low-latency routes, and configure route-level preemption/priorities, plus set a higher concurrency floor for short prompt route.
[00:02:03] Owen: what's preemption look like — can a small-short request interrupt a forming batch with long prompts?
[00:02:11] Jordan: not interrupt per se; we do priority-aware batching. you can flag requests as low_latency, and those get allowed into smaller, faster batches that have a different max_wait_ms and max_batch_size. that avoids the tailing effect.
[00:02:24] Lena: is that per-route config in the pilot UI or via config file? we want to automate in CI.
[00:02:30] Jordan: both — there's v2 route config accepted via API and an infra YAML for the private deployment. i'll attach examples.
[00:02:39] [00:02:40] Owen: ok, curious about max_inflight — we had it at 12 per GPU because previous guidance suggested 10-16 depending on model size. maybe we should increase?
[00:02:51] Diego: increasing helps throughput but can increase memory pressure (kv cache growth) — for your mix (mostly short + occasional long) we recommended trying max_inflight=24 with tight per-route batching for low-latency.
[00:03:05] Rajiv: any risks with 24, like OOMs?
[00:03:10] Diego: depends on model and quant. with your model (bfloat 8 quant) we have headroom but we need to watch total device memory and readahead. that's why we want logs from your stress run.
[00:03:21] Nina: when you say readahead — is that KV cache prefetching?
[00:03:24] Jordan: yeah KV cache + prefix caching behaviors. long contexts increase kv cache entries which can push eviction windows and impact new requests.
[00:03:34] [00:03:40] Nina: noted. what about queue_depth? we set a big value (1k) to avoid throttling — perhaps that backfired.
[00:03:48] Jordan: big queue_depth can hide congestion — it'll accept requests but increase tail latency. for your latency-sensitive route it's better to set a smaller queue_depth (e.g., 50) and use a soft-fallback to burst-capacity or an approximate model.
[00:04:01] Owen: is approximate model fallback supported today? we could route to a smaller quantized variant for sub-second responses.
[00:04:07] Maya: yes, we support model variants and automatic fallback policies — you can configure fallback on latency SLO breach to a faster quantized model or lower temperature to reduce tokens.
[00:04:18] [00:04:40] Rajiv: can you show us config examples? we want to see continuous_batching, priorities, max_inflight, queue_depth, and fallback rules in one file.
[00:04:48] Jordan: i'll put a snippet in the follow-up email. quick live pseudo: route.low_latency -> {max_wait_ms: 8, max_batch: 16, priority: high, queue_depth: 50, max_inflight: 24}, route.long_gen -> {max_wait_ms: 60, max_batch: 64, priority: low, queue_depth: 200}.
[00:05:10] Nina: that looks reasonable. one thing: we saw 502s come from the Nginx ingress when queue piled — is that a proxy timeout or Redwood dropping?
[00:05:19] Diego: probably proxy timeouts — if the upstream sits w/ long queuing, the edge proxy might close connections. we recommended tuning upstream_timeout + enabling streaming so the ingress doesn't wait for full generation.
[00:05:31] Lena: we use Envoy; will need to increase idle timeouts and also watch reset counts.
[00:05:36] Owen: can streaming help for long jobs to reduce perceived latency for users?
[00:05:40] Maya: streaming reduces TTFB for long generations and can reduce ingress timeouts, yes. also reduces client-side aborts that cascade.
[00:05:49] [00:06:00] Nina: last week you shared a dashboard that had "batch fill rate" and "batch latency P95" — can we get the formulas or the column definitions?
[00:06:09] Jordan: sure. batch fill rate = average fraction of batch slots used; batch_latency_p95 is from time of schedule->first token out. i'll attach a small doc.
[00:06:22] Rajiv: looking at the telemetry, one weird pattern: the dedicated pool had healthy GPU utilization but per-GPU stalls correlated with the times the long prompt jobs started — is there a kernel selection thrash?
[00:06:34] Diego: possible. model kernels switch when sequence length distribution changes; there's a tiny cost for switching kernels but normally it's negligible. if you have frequent alternation between short and long batches, we can pin scheduling to favor more consistent kernel shapes or warm some kernels.
[00:06:47] Owen: warm kernels? like keep an in-memory primed path for certain sequence lengths?
[00:06:51] Diego: yes, we'd allocate a small warm pool and schedule a soft reservation so a GPU doesn't repeatedly recompile or thrash kernels. this is higher-touch but worth it for mixed workloads.
[00:07:05] Nina: sounds heavier — what's the operational tradeoff?
[00:07:08] Diego: a bit more reserved memory, and slightly less absolute throughput in steady state, but much lower variance and fewer tail spikes.
[00:07:16] [00:07:40] Rajiv: ok, for the pilot, i'd rather reduce variance. let's try the max_inflight bump + smaller queue_depth + prioritize small requests, and if that still spikes, we look at kernel warm pools.
[00:07:53] Maya: agreed. Jordan, Diego — are we comfortable with the suggested defaults for ClearPort's traffic mix?
[00:07:58] Jordan: yes — propose two route templates: low_latency and long_gen. low_latency: max_wait_ms 8, max_batch 16, queue_depth 50, max_inflight 24, priority high. long_gen: max_wait_ms 60, max_batch 64, queue_depth 200, max_inflight 8, priority low. plus fallback: quantized model at 0.5x latency for long jobs when queue_depth>150.
[00:08:23] Nina: will the fallback change semantics? we rely on answer quality for some use cases.
[00:08:27] Maya: fallback should be for non-critical routes; we'll add a flag to only fallback for exploratory calls, not the canonical answers route.
[00:08:33] Owen: regarding telemetry for the stress run, what logs do you need? per-request traces, batch-level timing, GPU memory snapshots, and proxy reset counts?
[00:08:42] Jordan: that covers it. add kernel-switch events and batch composition histograms (short vs long). those tell us if batching is skewing.
[00:08:54] Lena: ok we'll export those. do you want them in CSV or the Prometheus format?
[00:08:59] Jordan: Prom is fine — but CSV for the batch-level histos is useful too.
[00:09:04] [00:09:40] Nina: one more item: we've budgeted pilot $$ for a burst capacity add-on — is there a stepped pricing for occasional burst capacity?
[00:09:49] Maya: yes, we have a burst capacity addon priced by vGPU-hour and a per-token premium during burst window. i'll send the pricing table; for your pilot we can do a small buffer with a negotiated rate.
[00:09:59] Rajiv: perfect. also curious about network egress — any changes with fallback and multi-model routing?
[00:10:05] Jordan: minimal — routing to a different model in the same pool is internal; cross-region fallback would add egress. we'll avoid cross-region for pilot.
[00:10:13] [00:10:40] Owen: can we run the stress test scenarios now or do you want us to use a schedule?
[00:10:45] Maya: schedule is fine — but make sure to run during low business hours and include a warmup period. also ensure the client doesn't retry aggressively on 5xxs, because retries mask the real backpressure.
[00:10:57] Nina: good call. we'll set no retries and use a 5m warmup then 60m steady. start with 2k rps smalls, 200 rps longs, then a step to 3k/400.
[00:11:12] Diego: we'll watch the pilot's dedicated pool while you run the test and capture kernel switches and memory.
[00:11:20] [00:11:40] Owen: any quick wins we can apply without a stress run? smaller queue_depth and route priority changes might be enough.
[00:11:46] Jordan: yes, apply route-level low_latency config first — that should buy you immediate reduction in P95 for small requests.
[00:11:52] Nina: let's do that today. Jordan, can you post the config?
[00:11:56] Jordan: yes i will.
[00:12:03] [00:12:40] Rajiv: wrapping up, the success criteria for next sync: 1) small-route P95 < 120ms under mixed load, 2) no unexplained 5xxs during the stress run, 3) documented fallback acceptance criteria.
[00:12:57] Maya: good. we'll also add a short checklist: update route config, run stress test, gather telemetry, review next week.
[00:13:10] Nina: thanks everyone — any other questions?
[00:13:15] Owen: one off — do you have recommendations for model quantization that preserves our ILR scores?
[00:13:22] Jordan: short answer: try int8 dynamic and run eval set; we have a quantization harness. we'll share recommended checkpoints.
[00:13:30] [00:14:00] Maya: cool. i'll send notes and config; Jordan will drop the telemetry keys and the example stress harness; Diego will watch for kernel thrash during the run.
[00:14:12] Nina: thanks, that was helpful.
[00:14:20] Rajiv: thanks.

[00:41:30] (call end)

Refs/Links mentioned: pilot telemetry sheet (shared), Redwood route config examples (will be attached), pilot pricing/burst addon doc (will be attached).

Auto-summary (end): proposed immediate change: apply low_latency route template and raise max_inflight for small route, set bounded queue_depth, schedule stress run, review results next week.
